stem: An arterial blood gas report shows a markedly negative base excess (base deficit). Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: It indicates a relative deficit of metabolic base and supports a metabolic acidifying component when interpreted with the full ABG.
options.B: It proves an isolated respiratory disorder with no metabolic contribution.
options.C: It is unrelated to metabolic acid-base interpretation.
options.D: It always represents normal acid-base balance regardless of the other ABG values.

rationale: Base excess/deficit is a calculated ABG parameter representing the relative excess or deficit of base. A markedly negative value represents a base deficit and supports a metabolic acidifying component, but ABG interpretation must still integrate pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate, and the clinical context. Therefore A is correct.
educational_objective: Interpret a negative base excess as evidence of a metabolic base deficit without using it as a standalone acid-base diagnosis.
source_document_title: Arterial Blood Gas Analysis: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Clinical Utility
source_locator: Specimen Requirements and Procedure — calculated base excess/deficit; Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings — systematic ABG interpretation
source_claim_supported: Base excess/deficit reflects relative excess or deficit of base; acid-base diagnosis requires integrated interpretation of pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate and other data.
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpretation of laboratory and diagnostic findings
correction_summary: Updated to the July 2026 StatPearls ABG chapter and softened the original overstatement from 'equals metabolic acidosis' to 'supports a metabolic acidifying component when interpreted with the full ABG.' Difficulty set to medium.
audit_findings: The updated NCBI chapter directly defines base excess/deficit and requires integrated ABG interpretation. A is appropriately qualified; B-D are false. Independent second pass passed.
